Jack takes one step toward her.
She shakes her head.
Don't.
He stops.
She looks at him. There is something almost childlike in her face now. Not rage. Disbelief. As though she is still hoping he will tell her that what she's heard is wrong.
She walks toward him. Slowly. One shoe, one bare foot on the wet road.
You knew.
Jack doesn't answer.
Her face changes. That silence is the answer.
She hits him. Not a big cinematic slap. One desperate blow against his chest with her fist.
He takes it.
She hits him again. Then again.
You knew where she was.
He says nothing. He can't. Behind his silence is a promise to a dead girl, and the audience knows it, and Vera doesn't.
She hits him again, weaker. And then the anger drains out of her all at once. Her hands just fall.
Why didn't you tell me?
Jack opens his mouth. Nothing comes.
She was waiting for me.
That line is almost inaudible.
Jack looks away.
And I was waiting for you.
And you were with her.
Jack closes his eyes.
And that is when Vera finally breaks. Not screaming. She simply folds. Her knees hit the wet pavement.
Jack drops down instinctively, reaching for her.
Her hands grab the front of his coat. She holds on. For one second it looks as if she is going to let him hold her.
Then she realises whose coat it is.
She pushes him away.
And sits there, in the rain, in the red dress.
Jack kneels a few feet away. He doesn't touch her again.
WIDE. EXTREME WIDE.
Two small figures on a huge, empty, shining street. The vending machines hum. The rain falls through their light.
Every sound drops away except the rain.

In the black water beside Vera, her reflection. And in the reflection, for less than a second, the street is slightly different: a shutter open that is closed, a warm light in a window that is dark, and a figure under a pale blue umbrella who could be Mara, or could be no one.
It is gone.
Vera covers her face with her hands.
Above them, an elevated train passes, a long ribbon of lit windows. Inside, strangers sleep, read, stare at their phones. Nobody looks down.
Only now does the SCORE enter: sparse and mournful, as if coming from very far away.
The shot holds. Long enough that it becomes hard to watch. There is nothing Jack can say. Nothing that fixes it.

scenes.title: 75 — Still frames — what the night left
scenes.prose: INT./EXT. VARIOUS - NIGHT - SERIES OF SHOTS

dialogueBeats.text: Still frames. No people.
— A single red high-heeled shoe lying in a puddle on an empty street, rain dimpling the water around it.
— The hotel lounge, empty, the chairs up. The pale blue umbrella still leaning against the bar stool.
— The Hive at night, the noodle shop shutter down, its old sign still faintly glowing.
— The vending machine on the empty street, humming, lit, waiting for no one.
— A small television in a shop window, showing only static.
— The pedestrian crossing from 27 and 62. Empty. The signal turns green for no one, and the old melody CHIMES across the wet street, all the way to the end.
Darkness. Rain on the window.
Vera sits on the floor with her back against the bed, still in the ruined red dress, mascara dried on her face. One shoe. The phone lights her face. A contact: MOM. She presses it.
Far away, in another morning, it's answered.
Vera? Honey?
Vera opens her mouth. Nothing comes.
Vera?
She ends the call. The screen goes dark.
In her hand, the old steel lighter.
She opens it. Closes it. Opens it.
She should throw it away. She holds it against her chest instead, and bends over it, and cries without making a sound.
She still loves him. She hates herself for it.
The desk lamp. Static on the TV. Jack sits in his wet coat at the desk. He still hasn't washed his hands.
On the desk: Daniel Voss's notebook.
He hears her voice. Over and over. Not the words from tonight. The words from the noodle counter at 11:40.
You're the first person I've trusted since she disappeared.

He opens the drawer. Takes out a clean envelope. Takes Sakai's letter from his coat, smooths it once more along its crease, and folds it inside the notebook's cover. Puts the notebook in the envelope.
He picks up a pen to write something on the envelope. He holds it over the paper for a long time.
He writes nothing.

scenes.title: 78 — No name
scenes.prose: EXT. VERA'S APARTMENT BUILDING, CORRIDOR - DAWN

dialogueBeats.text: Grey light. An open-air walkway along the third floor. Rain dripping from the railing.
Jack at Vera's door. He doesn't knock. He sets Daniel's notebook on the mat, squares it to the door, and goes.
Vera opens her door. She is still in the dress. She hasn't slept.
On the doormat: a plain envelope. No name.
She picks it up. Opens it. The cloth-covered notebook. And tucked inside its cover, a folded sheet of lined paper.
She sees the name inside the cover, and her whole body goes still.
DANIEL VOSS.
Vera sits at the low table in the dawn light. Beside her, the two cups from the beginning of the film, both empty now.
She unfolds the lined paper first.
Careful, laborious English handwriting. "Miss Voss. Your father did not kill himself. I can prove it."
It is the letter she threw away. Smoothed flat by someone else's hands.
She understands, all at once, why her sister was in a Kanda backstreet at one in the morning. Mara went to find the truth Vera refused to look at.
She sets the letter down very carefully, beside the empty cups. Then she opens the notebook and turns the pages.
Her father's handwriting. Neat, slanted, careful.
Shiohama. Third visit. The residents say men came in the spring with flowers, and then in the summer with iron bars. The fire began in two places at once. Fires don't do that.
She turns pages. The handwriting grows faster.
The claim will be paid. Everyone wants it paid. The company, the police, the man who owns the land now. Kurose. Always Kurose.
Pages.
The police have given me a young detective who speaks English. They call him Jack. He's bright. He believes me. We ate noodles at Kaneko's and I told him everything and he wrote it all down.
Vera stops. Reads that line again.
Her hand goes to her mouth.
She turns the page. The line we didn't see Jack read, underlined twice.
Today Jack signed the report. Accidental fire. I don't blame him. He is twenty-eight years old and they own his whole life. But I thought, of all of them, he would stand with me.
Vera stares at the page.
I'll go on alone. I've done it before.
The last pages. The handwriting is almost unrecognisable now.

They followed me home again tonight. The girls were asleep. I stood at the door a long time. If something happens to me, it will not be what they say. Tell Vera. When she is old enough. Tell her it will not be what they say.
Vera closes the notebook.
For twenty years she believed her father chose to leave her.
She sits in the grey light, holding the notebook against her chest, the way she held the lighter.
She has been given back her father and taken Jack away in the same hour. She doesn't know which to feel first.

scenes.title: 80 — Where to find them
scenes.prose: INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: Rows of cluttered desks, most of them empty: the shift change. Two young detectives at the far end, heads down over paperwork, too far away to hear. On the wall, the clock that runs a minute fast.
Ishida sits at his desk writing a report in careful longhand.
Jack walks the length of the room. The young detectives glance up and then look away. He hasn't shaved. There is still dried blood in the creases of his knuckles.
He stops at Ishida's desk. Ishida doesn't look up.
Nine o'clock. A grey car. Your driver.
Ishida finishes his sentence. Puts down the pen.
Only you knew.
A long pause.
You told me yourself, Jack. You always tell the wrong person.
Jack's hands close at his sides. The far end of the room has gone quiet.
Twenty years ago. Daniel. Was that you?
I have never killed anyone in my life. I only ever told people where to find them.
Jack looks at him for a long time. Ishida almost seems to want him to.
He doesn't.
Where is it? Sakai's thing.
Jack turns and walks away down the long room, past the desks, past the clock.
Ishida watches him go. For the first time, he looks afraid.
The bar in daylight. Chairs on the tables. Okada behind the counter.
He sees Jack's face and his hands, and he doesn't ask. He opens the cash drawer, lifts out the tray, and hands Jack the cassette.
Jack holds it.
The girl?
Jack can't answer.
Okada closes his eyes. Then he pours two small glasses and puts one in front of Jack. They drink together, without a toast.
An old newspaper office. Stacks of paper. Desks jammed together. Televisions on the walls showing three different channels. Nobody under fifty looks up from a screen.
In a glass-walled office at the back: HARADA (50s), the editor, grey-haired, sleeves rolled. On her desk, a framed photo of the JOURNALIST from the bar, laughing at some office party.
On the desk between them: an old cassette player, borrowed from somewhere, and the tape.
Harada presses PLAY.
Hiss. Then two men's voices, twenty years younger. Sakai's rough. The other one smooth, patient, faintly bored.
There are still people in the building. Old people. They won't sign.
The building must be empty by the end of the month.
And if it isn't?
Then it will be empty in a different way. Don't make me say it more clearly, Sakai. I don't like to repeat myself.
Harada stops the tape. The newsroom noise outside the glass seems very far away.
That's Kurose.
That's Kurose.
A voice on a twenty-year-old tape. His lawyers will say it's a fake. They'll say Sakai was a gangster with a grudge.
Then you'll need a witness.
She looks at him.

Twenty years ago I was a police detective. An American insurance investigator named Daniel Voss proved the Shiohama fire was arson. I believed him. I was ordered to close the case, and I signed a report saying the fire was an accident. Weeks later he was found dead. I didn't ask any questions.
You understand what you're saying. You'll be named. Your part too.
Start with my part.
Harada looks at him for a long moment. Then she looks at the photograph of her dead reporter on the desk. She takes a notebook from her drawer and opens it to a clean page.
From the beginning.
Jack begins to talk. We don't hear it. We watch him through the glass wall of her office, among the busy desks and flickering televisions: a man, for the first time in twenty years, not silent.

scenes.title: 82 — The notebook photocopied
scenes.prose: INT. TOTO SHIMBUN NEWSROOM, CORRIDOR - LATER

dialogueBeats.text: Vera stands at the edge of the newsroom with a plain folder under her arm and her father's notebook in both hands. Through the glass wall of the office at the back, Jack, talking. She can't hear him. She has never seen him say anything true in that voice.
She doesn't go in.

A YOUNG COPY CLERK at a photocopier lays the notebook open under the lid and presses the button. A bar of light passes under the page: her father's handwriting, flashing white. Turn. Press. Turn. Press.
Harada comes out of the office and pulls the door closed behind her.
Two hours. He hasn't stopped.
I know. I can see.
Harada watches the pages come out of the machine.
Every page. Then the original goes in the safe downstairs, and nobody touches it. Including you.
It's all I have of him.

Then I will take care of it. Kondo's files were in his desk. Six months of redevelopment money, and Kurose's name in most of it. And the grey car that left the Hive last night was found burnt out in Adachi at dawn. Registered to a security company. The company belongs to Kurose Development. Tomorrow we put it to them for comment. They will refuse to see a reporter.
I'll go.
That is not your job.
It isn't yours either. He'll see me. He'll want to look at me.
Harada studies her. Then hands her the folder: a stack of photocopies, warm from the machine.
The copies. Not the original.

scenes.title: 83 — It's just a face
scenes.prose: INT. CHAIRMAN'S OFFICE, KUROSE DEVELOPMENT - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: The fortieth floor. Rain on the glass. Tokyo grey and endless below.
Vera sits in a leather chair in front of Kurose's desk. She wears a plain dark coat. A plain folder is on her lap, her hands flat on its cover: photocopies of every page of her father's notebook.
Across from her sits THE CHAIRMAN, KUROSE (70s). Silver hair. A beautiful suit. The stillness of a man who has never had to hurry.
Courteous. Curious. He pours her tea himself.
When my secretary said the daughter of Daniel Voss wanted to see me, I didn't believe her.
His English is perfect. Old-fashioned.
He sat where you're sitting. He looked at me the way you are. As if I'd done something.
Did you?
To him? I don't remember. Your father was a good man, Miss Voss. I mean that sincerely. There are not many. Good men are very expensive.
Vera doesn't touch the tea.
What is it you want?
He takes a plain envelope, thick with cash, from a drawer and lays it on the glass between them. She doesn't look at it.
The Toto Shimbun will print tomorrow. They asked me to bring you the chance to reply.
And they sent you.
I said I'd come.
Why?
I wanted to see your face.
And?
It's just a face.
For the first time, something flickers in him. Not fear. Irritation, perhaps, at being looked at like that.
Vera stands. She holds up a page of the photocopy. Not threatening. Just showing it to him.
My father kept notes. He wrote your name on every page. And now I know.
She walks to the door. On her way out, she stops at the model. Where the Hive stood, there's only the white plaza. Tiny painted people cross it.
It's very clean.
She goes.
Kurose sits still for a moment. Then he presses a button on his desk phone.
Follow her.

scenes.title: 84 — Three feet away
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, NOODLE SHOP STOREROOM - NIGHT

dialogueBeats.text: The bulb. The flour sacks. The futon, folded now. On it, a neat stack of drawings, dried flat, their edges rippled from the wet floor.
Jack sits on the floor against the wall. He has been hiding here since the newspaper; he can't go home. His face is grey with exhaustion.
The curtain opens. Kaneko.
Someone for you.
She stands aside.
Vera.
Jack gets to his feet. Neither of them moves toward the other.
She asked me to come. Kaneko. She said I should see where Mara was.
In her hands, a small cloth bag with one strap frayed. Kaneko put it there at the door.

She looks around the tiny room. The bare bulb. The flour sacks. And on the wall, taped up with rice-paper tape, pages from Mara's sketchbook: drawings of the noodle counter, but from the inside now. From behind the curtain. The back of a head.
Vera walks to the wall. Looks at the drawing for a long time.
That's me.
She drew it after you left.
She was here. The day I came.
Three feet away.
Vera touches the paper with one finger.
And you told her not to come out.
She told herself. She was protecting you. So was I.
Ishida called me before it was on any news. He knew exactly where she was.
I told him. Where she'd be, and when. He arranged the car. It was his driver. That's mine.
I told you about the detective. The one who promised a car. You never asked who.
No.
Vera says nothing for a while. She does not say it's all right.
I'm not going to tell you it wasn't yours.
Don't.

She opens the bag. Folded pages, soft with handling. She smooths one flat on the flour sack: a counter seen from the floor. Two pairs of shoes. A stool going over. A hand. Beside the shoes, in block capitals: EXCUSE ME.
She drew what she saw. All of it.
She never told me she'd kept them.
I'm taking these to Harada. Somebody has to look at them. I read his notebook.
I know.
He didn't blame you.
I know.
I don't know if I'm as good as he was.
I'm not asking you to be.
Silence. A train passes overhead. The bulb swings.
And under the train, so quietly it's almost part of it: in the passage outside, a man's voice, murmuring into his sleeve.
Position.
Jack's head snaps round. Vera sees his face and understands.
The bulb goes on swinging.
Three hard strikes, iron on iron, run up the pipes overhead. Then again, farther off: a spoon on a radiator, a knuckle on a drainpipe, floor above floor. The Hive is passing it on.
Four masked men move through the narrow corridors in single file, weapons up. The passages are too narrow for anything else.
Doors that stood open close softly, one after another, as they pass. The Hive is watching them.
Kaneko lowers the ladle from the old iron water pipe by the stove. Three strikes were all it took: the alarm the Hive has kept for fifty years.
Kaneko pulls the shutter down with a crash. She turns off the fluorescent tube.
Up. Through the back. The stairs by the dentist. Then go through the neighbours. Everyone will open a door.
I know them.
Jack looks at her.
Come with us.
I have lived here fifty years. They can come and find me.
Go now. They will help you.
She pushes them toward the back.

scenes.title: 87 — The main switch
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, RADIO REPAIR SHOP - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: The pipes have already told him. The RADIO REPAIRMAN looks up from his bench at the sound of boots in the corridor. He looks at the old fuse box on his wall.
He reaches up and pulls the main switch.
DARK.
In the black, Vera's hand finds the wall, low, where a child's hand would reach. She starts to move. Jack follows the sound of her.
Every bulb in the building goes out at once.
The masked men stop. Flashlights snap on, tight white beams in the narrow corridors, catching dripping pipes, closed doors, laundry, faces at windows that vanish the moment the light touches them.
The Hive knows its own dark. The men don't.
Pitch black. A narrow concrete stair.
Vera climbs by touch, one hand on the wall. Her other hand finds Jack's and pulls him up after her.
Halfway up, she stops. Takes the lighter out of her pocket. Her thumb on the wheel.
Below them: boots. A flashlight beam crawls up the wall and falls away.
She puts the lighter back unlit, and climbs.

scenes.title: 90 — Through the rooms
scenes.prose: INT. THE HIVE, THROUGH THE ROOMS - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: Vera leads them to a door with a sumo match murmuring behind it. It opens before she can knock: the OLD WOMAN from 55.
The old woman's room. A sumo match murmurs on a television nobody is watching. She points across it to the far wall, where a second door stands open.

Beyond it, another room. A kitchen in the dark, lit by one candle: the FAMILY around the table, the father with the baseball bat across his knees, the children holding the next door wide. Beyond that, the dentist's chair, the dentist with a finger to his lips. A bedroom where the girl with the violin sits up, the instrument held against her chest like a child.
A passage that is really the inside of someone's wardrobe.

Through the wardrobe, a barber's cramped shop. The BARBER holds the beaded curtain aside with his scissors hand and turns the chair to the wall, so that anyone looking in will see only a man waiting for a haircut.

Down four steps into a laundry where wet sheets hang in rows. Two WOMEN part the sheets ahead of them and pin them shut again behind, so that the whole room closes like water over the place they went.

A shrine room. A GRANDMOTHER lifts the altar cloth and a low hatch opens behind it. She holds the cloth until they are through, then smooths it flat over the candle and the photograph as if nothing had happened.

A plank laid across the gap between two balconies, a balcony bolted onto a balcony. Two MEN in vests steady it at both ends, and when the last of them is across, haul it in after them, so that the gap is only a gap.
A pipe gallery, the pipes ringing softly all around them. A WOMAN raps one pipe once for clear, and the next hand takes it up farther on: the alarm still passing, now telling them which way is safe.
At every door, someone. A hand. A nod. A lantern turned low. Nobody speaks. Nobody looks at Vera or at Jack. They pass through other people's lives like water through a wall.
Behind them, each door closes softly. In the passage beyond, a flashlight beam finds each closed door in turn, and stops.
The Hive is closing behind them the way it opened for the masked men, only the other way round.
The last room is in the rear wing, and it is empty: a window over the foot of the viaduct, its shutter open. An iron fire ladder bolted to the wall outside, going down into the dark.

scenes.title: 91 — The ladder under the train
scenes.prose: EXT. THE HIVE, REAR WALL BY THE VIADUCT - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: Rain. The rear wall of the low wing, pressed against the concrete viaduct. Vera comes out of the window onto the ladder. Jack after her, pulling the shutter to behind him.
Above, a flashlight beam sweeps the window and finds only a closed shutter.
Overhead the rails begin to sing. A light grows at the far end of the viaduct.

A train. It arrives, a roaring wall of noise and wind and lit windows, and under it the two of them go down the ladder, rung by rung, and nobody hears a thing. Passengers inside reading, sleeping, looking at their phones. None of them see.
Her hand is in his on the rail. At the bottom she doesn't take it back.
When the last carriage has passed, the ladder is empty.

scenes.title: 92 — Until us
scenes.prose: EXT. STREET BELOW THE VIADUCT - MOMENTS LATER

dialogueBeats.text: Vera and Jack step off the last rung of the fire ladder into an empty street. Soaked. Breathing hard.
Behind them, the Hive: every window lit again now, every radio playing, every resident awake. In the distance, sirens.
Vera steps away from him. Just one step. Enough.
They look at each other in the rain. There is too much to say, and none of it can be said tonight.
Is Kaneko —
The Hive looks after its own.
She nods. She looks up at the building full of light.
Mara was safe here. Until us.
He has no answer to that. She doesn't need one.
Rain. Ishida comes down the front steps without an umbrella.
At the kerb, a black sedan. Engine running. Wipers beating slowly.
He stops. He knows this car.
A long moment. Then the rear door opens from inside.

scenes.title: 94 — The lit window
scenes.prose: EXT. POLICE STATION / INT. BLACK SEDAN - CONTINUOUS

dialogueBeats.text: At the foot of the steps, a black sedan waits at the kerb, engine running, wipers going.
The rear door opens from inside. Warm amber light. Leather.
Ishida stops in the rain. He looks back up at the station, at one lit window on the second floor where somebody is still working.
From inside the car, a man's clean hand holds out a cup of tea. The watch from the model.
It's only tea.
Ishida gets in. The door closes. The rain is suddenly very far away.
The black car recedes down a long wet road, its taillights smearing red, exactly like the car in the first scene of the film.
It turns a corner. Gone.

scenes.title: 96 — A minute fast
scenes.prose: INT. POLICE STATION, DETECTIVES' ROOM - MORNING

dialogueBeats.text: Grey daylight. A cardboard box on Ishida's desk. A young detective is clearing it.
He opens the bottom drawer. Empty.
The desk phone rings. He picks it up.
Yes. Where? In his own car. Under the expressway. Sitting up, engine off. No marks. He left a statement.
He puts the phone down very slowly. He looks at the empty chair. At the empty drawer.
On the wall, the clock still runs a minute fast.

scenes.title: 98 — The rain has stopped
scenes.prose: EXT. ROOFTOP OF JACK'S BUILDING - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: FIVE DAYS LATER
Days later. The rain has stopped for the first time in the film. The sky is pale and washed and enormous.
A small flat roof: laundry poles, a water tank, a single potted plant someone has kept alive. Below, the elevated railway, and the trains going past at eye level.
Jack stands at the railing. He hears the door behind him.
Vera. In a plain coat. Her hair dry.
She comes to stand beside him at the railing. Not close. Not far.
Harada says the prosecutors want you to testify.
Yes.
And your licence?
Gone. It should have gone twenty years ago.
Ishida left a statement. He acted alone.
Is that what it says?
That's what the police say it says.
Harada has Mara's drawings. The pages from the floor of the bar. She says they're the only eyewitness there is.
She'd have liked that. Being asked.
Nobody asked her. She drew it anyway.
A train passes below. They watch it.
Jack takes something from his pocket. Holds it out on his open palm.
The red bird clip.
This is yours.
Vera looks at it. She takes it.
She said your father gave it to her. She said you only claim it was yours.
Vera laughs. It comes out broken.
Liar. It was mine.
She closes her hand around it.
Jack looks at the trains. It is the hardest thing he will ever say, and he says it simply.
At the end, she asked me to tell you something.
Vera goes very still.
She said to tell you she was sorry.
Vera stares at him.
And then she understands. Not the words. What they mean. The fight. The last cruel things she said at the door. The flight home. Everything she has carried since the first scene.
Mara wasn't angry. Mara had forgiven her the whole time.
Vera turns away to the railing. Her shoulders shake. Jack doesn't touch her. He stands beside her while she cries, the way he knelt beside her in the rain. Close enough. Not closer.
When she can speak:
You could have told me that in the rain.
I couldn't say anything in the rain.
No. Neither could I.
A train. They watch it pass.
I don't know what we are.
Neither do I.
I still have your lighter.
I know.
She takes it from her coat pocket. Looks at it. Opens it. Closes it.
She doesn't give it back. She puts it away again.
Kaneko's opening a new place. Near the station, under the arches. She's taking the sign.
She walks to the rooftop door. Stops. Doesn't look back.
She says she opens at six.
She goes.
Jack stands alone at the railing. A train passes, its windows full of people. For a moment, in one of the windows, the reflection of his own face.

scenes.title: 99 — The Hive coming down, then the plaza
scenes.prose: EXT. THE HIVE / THE PLAZA, WHERE THE HIVE WAS - DAY

dialogueBeats.text: Weeks later.
The Hive is coming down.
Excavators bite into the walls with long steel jaws. Concrete falls in slow grey curtains. Dust hangs in the air.

The building has been cut open like the illustrated cross-sections in an old book. Rooms stand exposed to the sky, stacked one above another: a wall of flowered wallpaper, a calendar still pinned beside a window, a mirror, a child's height marks pencilled on a doorframe.
The camera tracks slowly sideways along the ruined face of the building, as it tracked along the lit windows of the living one. Empty room after empty room. We remember who lived in each.
At ground level, Kaneko's counter is still standing. Its six old stools in a row.
At the barrier on the street, a small crowd watches. The radio repairman. The family. The girl with the violin case.
Kaneko stands among them, holding the old noodle-shop sign against her chest, wrapped in a blanket.
Months later. Winter light, thin and clear. No rain.
The white plaza from the model, built. Real people cross it now, exactly like the painted ones. A strip of new grass. A bench nobody sits on.
Nothing marks where anything was.
A tiny place in a brick railway arch near the station. Steam. One warm bulb.
Above the counter, the old hand-painted sign. Faded. Unmistakable.
A train goes over. The bottles tick against each other and settle.

On a shelf above the door, a small old television with the sound down: the evening news. KUROSE walking into a building between lawyers, cameras flashing, his face composed. A photograph of ISHIDA in uniform. Then the weather.
Nobody looks up.
Kaneko ladles. JACK sits at the counter, a bowl in front of him, a space beside him.
The curtain in the doorway moves. VERA. The red bird clip in her hair.
She stands a moment. Then she sits down beside him.
Kaneko sets a bowl in front of her. Vera eats. All of it.
She puts money on the counter. Too much. Kaneko looks at it, then at her, and leaves it where it is.
Past the curtain: a lit window, a radio through a wall, the city going on.
HOLD on the three of them in the steam.
